phrases.cultural_context: 'Ayubowan' and 'Vanakkam' mean 'may you live long.' Often accompanied by a slight bow and palms pressed together.
phrases.usage_tips: Formal greeting suitable for any occasion. Shows respect and cultural awareness.

phrases.cultural_context: Used from sunrise until around 10 AM.
phrases.usage_tips: Perfect for greeting shop owners, hotel staff, or locals you meet in the morning.

phrases.cultural_context: Used from around 4 PM onwards.
phrases.usage_tips: Great for evening greetings at restaurants or when meeting people after work hours.

phrases.cultural_context: Used when parting in the evening or before sleep.
phrases.usage_tips: Say this when leaving a restaurant at night or when checking into your hotel.

phrases.cultural_context: Common casual greeting. Expect 'Hari hondai' (I'm fine) as a response.
phrases.usage_tips: Use with people you've met before or in casual conversations.

phrases.pronunciation: HA-ri, bo-HO-ma sthu-thi / naan nan-draa-ga i-ruk-ki-ren nan-dri
phrases.cultural_context: Standard polite response to 'How are you?'
phrases.usage_tips: Always respond with this to show politeness and respect.

phrases.cultural_context: One of the most important phrases. Locals appreciate gratitude.
phrases.usage_tips: Use frequently! After receiving help, service, or gifts.

phrases.cultural_context: In Sinhala, 'please' usually comes at the beginning of requests, not the end.
phrases.usage_tips: Essential for polite requests. Shows respect and good manners.

phrases.cultural_context: Use to apologize or get someone's attention politely.
phrases.usage_tips: Essential before asking for directions or interrupting someone.

phrases.pronunciation: o-yaa in-gri-si ka-thaa ka-ra-na-wa-da / neen-gal aan-gi-lam pe-su-veer-ga-la
phrases.cultural_context: Many Sri Lankans speak at least basic English, especially in tourist areas.
phrases.usage_tips: Use this before launching into complex questions.

phrases.cultural_context: Honesty is appreciated. People will often find someone who speaks English to help.
phrases.usage_tips: Don't be shy to use this. It helps avoid misunderstandings.

phrases.pronunciation: sæn-ta ka-thaa ka-ran-na / me-dhu pe-sa ven-dum
phrases.cultural_context: People will happily slow down for you.
phrases.usage_tips: Combine with 'I don't understand' when struggling with fast speech.

phrases.cultural_context: Response to 'thank you.' Often accompanied by a smile.
phrases.usage_tips: Use after someone thanks you for help or service.

phrases.cultural_context: Casual way to say goodbye, literally 'going and coming.'
phrases.usage_tips: Use with people you'll likely see again soon.

phrases.english: Excuse me, can you help me?
phrases.pronunciation: sa-maa-wen-na ma-ta u-daw ka-ran-na-da / man-nik-ka-vum e-nak-ku u-dha-vi sei-veer-ga-la
phrases.cultural_context: Always start by getting attention politely before asking for help.
phrases.usage_tips: Use before asking for directions or assistance.

phrases.pronunciation: bath ka-ma-rey ko-he-da / ka-zhi-vi-na a-rai en-gae
phrases.cultural_context: Essential phrase. Don't be embarrassed to ask.
phrases.usage_tips: Very useful in restaurants, shops, and public places.

phrases.cultural_context: Locals are very helpful with directions.
phrases.usage_tips: Point to a map or show hotel name on phone for clarity.

phrases.pronunciation: po-lis stha-na-ya ko-he-da / po-lis sta-tion en-gae
phrases.cultural_context: For emergencies, call 119 or 1912 (Tourist Police).
phrases.usage_tips: Hopefully you won't need this, but good to know.

phrases.pronunciation: me-nu e-kak la-ba gan-na pu-lu-wan-da / me-nu kat-ti-dam ku-dun-ga
phrases.cultural_context: Many restaurants have picture menus for tourists.
phrases.usage_tips: First step when dining out. Look for pictures if language is a barrier.

phrases.cultural_context: Specify if you want bottled water. Tap water isn't always safe for tourists.
phrases.usage_tips: Always ask for 'bottle water' if concerned about water quality.

phrases.cultural_context: Tipping is appreciated but not mandatory (5-10% is generous).
phrases.usage_tips: Make the universal hand-writing gesture along with this phrase.

phrases.cultural_context: Sri Lanka has many vegetarian options. Many restaurants cater to vegetarians.
phrases.usage_tips: Use early in the conversation. Staff will guide you to suitable dishes.

phrases.pronunciation: kau-lau ba-du tæ-va-raa / kaa-ra-mil-lai da-ya-vu sei-thu
phrases.cultural_context: Sri Lankan food can be very spicy. Don't hesitate to ask for mild versions.
phrases.usage_tips: Say this when ordering. You can also gesture 'little' with fingers.

phrases.cultural_context: Compliments are always appreciated and will earn you smiles.
phrases.usage_tips: Use with a smile to show genuine appreciation for the food.

phrases.cultural_context: Essential for shopping. Always ask the price first.
phrases.usage_tips: Point to item while asking. Expect prices in rupees (LKR).

phrases.cultural_context: Bargaining is common and expected in markets.
phrases.usage_tips: Say with a friendly smile to open negotiation, not confrontationally.

phrases.pronunciation: o-ba a-du ka-ran-na pu-lu-wan-da / vi-lai-yai ku-raik-ka mu-di-yu-maa
phrases.cultural_context: Polite negotiation is part of shopping culture.
phrases.usage_tips: Use after expressing that price is too high. Start at 50-70% of asking price.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ma me gan-na o-ne / i-thai vaan-ga vi-rum-bu-ki-ren
phrases.cultural_context: Use after agreeing on price.
phrases.usage_tips: Point to item clearly. Have money ready.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ma ba-lan-na ya-na-va / naan sum-ma paar-kki-ren
phrases.cultural_context: Vendors can be persistent. This politely declines without offense.
phrases.usage_tips: Use with a smile when browsing without intent to buy.

phrases.cultural_context: Shout loudly in emergencies. People will respond immediately.
phrases.usage_tips: Use only in genuine emergencies. Very effective.

phrases.pronunciation: po-li-si-ya-wa call ka-ran-na / po-lis-ku phone sei-yun-gal
phrases.cultural_context: Emergency number is 119. Tourist Police is 1912 (English-speaking).
phrases.usage_tips: Point to your phone while saying this. Someone will help call.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ma dos-ta-ra ba-lan-na o-ne / e-nak-ku doc-tor the-vai
phrases.cultural_context: Medical care is widely available. Locals will direct you to nearest hospital.
phrases.usage_tips: Point to affected body part. Say 'hospital' if very urgent.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ma ni-va-na-ta ya-na-wa / naan tho-lain-dhu poi-tten
phrases.cultural_context: Sri Lankans are very helpful. They'll often escort you or call someone.
phrases.usage_tips: Show hotel address or location on map. People will guide you.

phrases.pronunciation: bus stand e-ka ko-he-da / bus ni-la-yam en-ga
phrases.cultural_context: Buses are main public transport. Often crowded but very affordable.
phrases.usage_tips: Ask locals or show bus number. They'll point you to the right place.

phrases.pronunciation: dum-ri-ya sthaa-na-ya ko-he-da / ra-yil ni-lai-yam en-gae
phrases.cultural_context: Train journeys are scenic and worth experiencing.
phrases.usage_tips: Book 2nd or 3rd class for authentic local experience.

phrases.english: How much to go to the airport?
phrases.pronunciation: air-port-ta kee-ye-da / vi-maa-na ni-lai-yam sel-la ev-va-la-vu
phrases.cultural_context: Always agree on fare before starting journey. Use meter if available.
phrases.usage_tips: Research typical fares beforehand. Negotiate firmly but politely.

phrases.pronunciation: me-he na-wan-na ka-ru-naa-ka-ra / in-ga ni-ru-thun-go da-ya-vu sei-thu
phrases.cultural_context: Say clearly when you reach destination. Have money ready.
phrases.usage_tips: Point to location or landmark. Pay exact fare if possible.

etiquette_tips.title: Remove Footwear
etiquette_tips.description: Always remove shoes and hats before entering any Buddhist or Hindu temple. Leave them at the designated area.
dont_list: Step on temple steps with footwear

etiquette_tips.title: Dress Modestly
etiquette_tips.description: Cover shoulders and knees. Avoid revealing or tight-fitting clothing when visiting religious sites.

etiquette_tips.title: Respect Buddha Images
etiquette_tips.description: Never turn your back to a Buddha statue for photos. Don't touch or climb on religious monuments.

etiquette_tips.title: Observe Silence
etiquette_tips.description: Maintain quiet and peaceful behavior. Lower your voice and avoid loud conversations.

etiquette_tips.title: Palms Together Greeting
etiquette_tips.description: When saying 'Ayubowan', place your palms together at chest height in a prayer-like gesture. A slight bow of the head shows deeper respect.

etiquette_tips.title: Use Right Hand
etiquette_tips.description: When eating with hands, use only your right hand. The left hand is considered unclean.
dont_list: Touch communal dishes with left hand

etiquette_tips.title: Point with Chin
etiquette_tips.description: Pointing with fingers is considered rude. Use your chin or open palm to indicate direction.

etiquette_tips.title: Avoid Public Displays
etiquette_tips.description: Public displays of affection are frowned upon in Sri Lankan culture. Be respectful in public spaces.

cultural_notes.title: Greeting Customs
cultural_notes.content: 'Ayubowan' (Sinhala) and 'Vanakkam' (Tamil) are formal greetings meaning 'may you live long,' often accompanied by a slight bow and palms pressed together. This shows respect and is appreciated more than a simple handshake.

cultural_notes.title: Politeness Matters
cultural_notes.content: Sri Lankans value politeness. Always start requests with 'please' (karunakarala in Sinhala, dayavu seithu in Tamil). Even basic attempts to speak the local language will be warmly received.

cultural_notes.title: Bargaining Culture
cultural_notes.content: Bargaining is expected in local markets and with tuk-tuk drivers. Start at 50-70% of the asking price and negotiate with a smile. Stay friendly – it's part of the cultural experience!

cultural_notes.title: Emergency Numbers
cultural_notes.content: Keep these numbers saved: 119 (Police Emergency), 110 or 1990 (Ambulance), 1912 (Tourist Police - English-speaking). The Tourist Police are especially helpful for travelers.

cultural_notes.title: Temple Dress Code
cultural_notes.content: When visiting temples, cover shoulders and knees, remove footwear, and never turn your back to Buddha statues for photos. This shows respect for local religious customs.

cultural_notes.title: Spice Levels
cultural_notes.content: Sri Lankan cuisine can be very spicy. Don't hesitate to ask for 'no spice' (Kauḷau baḍu tævarā in Sinhala or Kāramillai in Tamil) when ordering. Restaurants are happy to accommodate.
